chapter_theme: Madhavi's answering shore songs end and the union breaks: she sings, in the voice of the akam heroine, of the tide that wiped out the lover's chariot tracks, the mother who may find out, three evenings asked whether they reach the absent man's land, a man who spoiled their sand-play, and, after changing mode, evening as killer and besieger, closing with a plea to the sea god to pardon a false oath; Kovalan hears the songs as her love for another, and the narrator, giving it to his ripening former deed, has him leave her on the shore.

cast.role: the dancer-courtesan of Puhar with whom Kovalan lived, who sings the second set of shore songs
merchant of Puhar, Kannaki's husband, who hears Madhavi's songs and leaves her
Kovalan's servants, who go with him from the shore
the god of the sea, addressed in the last song

silappathikaram:7:210-213.reading: The third stanza of the song to the tide: the singer hails the sea tide that ran over and broke the track her lover's tall wheeled chariot made, and says that it seemed to have done with her but has not.
silappathikaram:7:210-213.nuance: The three stanzas (202 to 213) turn on one image: the wheel ruts are the only trace the man left, and the tide that wipes them takes even that. The last line (எம்மொடு தீர்ந்தாய்போல் தீர்ந்திலையால்) can be read as the tide seeming to leave with him yet staying to torment her, or as its harm seeming finished and not being so; the unit does not fix which.

silappathikaram:7:214-221.reading: In a stanza of mixed landscapes the singer hails the lord of the shore, where the waves, wearing pearls and coral, roam even the red-paddy fields, and asks what she will do if her mother sees the fresh wounds that the god of the fish banner shot into her in the punnai grove, wounds she hid by her own guile.
silappathikaram:7:214-221.nuance: The sea decked in pearl and coral reaches into the paddy fields, which is why the rubric calls these stanzas மயங்கு திணை, mixed landscapes. The heroine fears not the wound but its discovery by the mother, the akam fear of secret love becoming known.

silappathikaram:7:222-229.reading: The second stanza hails the shore where the sea smiles with pearls and opens coral lips before the fishers' net-yards, and asks what she will do if her mother, seeing the girl take the colour of the rain-season peerku flower, decides a god has done this cruelty.
silappathikaram:7:222-229.nuance: The pallor likened to peerku blossom is the sign of love-sickness, and the feared misreading (கடவுள் வரைந்து, settling it on a god) is the akam mother's mistake that leads to the frenzy rite; the stanza names the mistake without the rite. The phrase is compressed, and its sense as 'the mother fixing on a god as cause' is a reading.

silappathikaram:7:230-237.reading: The third stanza hails the shore whose waves, grieving at their own fish smell, enter the cool grove and come away fragrant with fallen flowers, and asks what she will do if her mother learns of the unknown sickness the girl suffers alone, a longing that no single cause makes firm.
silappathikaram:7:230-237.nuance: The waves cure their own smell in the grove while the girl's sickness has no cure; பலஉற்று ஒருநோய் திணியாத suggests a sickness built of many pains that no one name fits, which is why the mother could not read it.

silappathikaram:7:238-241.reading: The singer tells her companion, woman of loosened flower-hair, that young darkness has spread, the sun has hidden and her eyes pour unstoppable tears, and asks whether this bewildering evening, which came scattering fire and loosening her bangles, exists in the land of the man who left.
silappathikaram:7:238-241.nuance: The question is barbed: if evening came to his land too, he would feel what she feels and come back. The song is sung to a lover who sits beside her, and the absent man is a persona, which is the ambiguity Kovalan will hear as a confession.

silappathikaram:7:242-245.reading: The second stanza repeats the complaint, the sun gone and dark cloud spreading, the eyes like opposed flowers shedding tears of pain, and asks the moon-faced companion whether this evening, which spat out the moon and swallowed the sun, is found in the land of the one who went.

silappathikaram:7:246-249.reading: The third stanza adds that the birds' songs have stopped and the full moon sharpens her sickness, and asks whether this evening, which came like an enemy upon her life, exists in the land of the one who abandoned her.
silappathikaram:7:246-249.nuance: The verb for the man hardens across the three stanzas, from தணந்தார் (who went apart) to போனார் (who went) to துறந்தார் (who abandoned).

silappathikaram:7:250-253.reading: In the first stanza of the saayal vari the singer tells her companion that a man came by the backwater fenced with screw-pine, spoiled their sand-play and went, and that he will not leave their infatuated heart.
silappathikaram:7:250-253.nuance: The repetition of the second line in the third is the form's refrain, and it turns the closing claim into a double meaning: he will not leave the heart, though he has left the place.

silappathikaram:7:254-257.reading: The second stanza says that a man came by the backwater fenced with the shore grove and stood saying 'grant me grace', and that he will not forget their deer-like glance.

silappathikaram:7:258-261.reading: The third stanza says that a man stood yesterday gazing as a swan played with its mate, and that he will not leave the golden freckles on her breast.
silappathikaram:7:258-261.nuance: The man who watched mated swans has learned the lesson of pairing, which is the stanza's hint that he will return.

silappathikaram:7:262-265.reading: The singer bids the heron not to settle in their shore grove, repeating the bidding, because it did not tell the lord of the breaking waves the sickness she suffers.
silappathikaram:7:262-265.nuance: The heron is refused for failing as a messenger; the doubled line 263 is the refrain of the form.

silappathikaram:7:266-269.reading: The narrator says that the woman of fine jewels, having sung thus, then raised on the yazh, with her soft kaanthal-like fingers, the sweet sevvazhi palai set on kaikkilai and kural, and sang by its rules, changing to another mode.
silappathikaram:7:266-269.nuance: The change of mode marks a change of mood: the songs that follow are evening laments in a mode of grief, and the narrator records it as a musician's choice before the reader learns what Kovalan makes of it.
silappathikaram:7:266-269.event: Madhavi finishes the shore songs and shifts the yazh to another mode for the evening songs.

silappathikaram:7:270-273.reading: The singer tells evening that it has struck the sweet palai the fisherfolk sing in vilari so that it settles in ili and kilai, and says that if it is so skilled in melody it may take her life.
silappathikaram:7:270-273.nuance: Evening is addressed as a fellow musician, and the musical terms (விளரி, இளி, கிளை) describe how the shore's own songs sound at dusk; how exactly the modes are meant to change is beyond what the lines settle.

silappathikaram:7:274-277.reading: The singer tells evening that it stands outside the lives of those who live pining in the shade of the great grace the departed lover tenderly promised, and asks what it will be, so placed, if not a king outside the fort against a king within who cannot hold out.
silappathikaram:7:274-277.nuance: The image is a siege: the woman's life is a fort whose inner king, weakened, cannot resist the king camped outside its wall, and the promise of grace is her only shelter. The construction of the last line is compressed and the reading of it as a siege is offered as a reading.

silappathikaram:7:278-281.reading: The singer says that as her grief grows and the sun goes down, bewildering evening comes and the world shuts its eyes, and that if this is what evening is and this is what the man who wed her is, the world itself has become poor.

silappathikaram:7:282-285.reading: The singer, in the last song, says that with these words of grief spoken without weighing them in this bewildering evening that came like fire, she bows at the flower feet of the god of the great sea and asks it to bear the false oath sworn in the fragrant grove.
silappathikaram:7:282-285.nuance: The plea presumes that the sea god punishes a false oath sworn before it, and the heroine asks it to hold its hand: she shields the man who lied. Line 284 reads கனலில் (in the fire); the sense of the grove (கானல்) suits the song cycle, and the text may be faulty here. Whose false oath is meant is not said, which is the opening for Kovalan's reading of the song as Madhavi's own.

silappathikaram:7:286-300.reading: The narrator says that Kovalan, hearing this, thought that while he had sung the shore songs she, her mind on another, had sung as a woman of lying tricks, and because his former deed had come in wrath through the yazh music he loosened his embrace and, saying the time had passed, left with his servants while she stayed seated, and Madhavi, her heart helpless, quieted her company in the flower grove and went home in her carriage without her lover, while the Chola's garlanded white umbrella shaded the earth.
silappathikaram:7:286-300.nuance: Two causes are given in one sentence: Kovalan's own judgement of the song (lines 287 to 288, in his voice) and the narrator's ஊழ்வினை வந்து உருத்தது (line 289), the patikam's own phrase for karma. The narrator does not say Madhavi had another in mind; the hidden intent exists only in Kovalan's reading. The closing four lines, opened by ஆங்கு, end the kaathai with a blessing on the Chola king and are not part of the scene.
silappathikaram:7:286-300.event: Kovalan, deciding Madhavi's songs betray love for another, leaves her on the shore, and she goes home alone.

claims.claim: a former deed comes in wrath and turns a man against the woman he loves

links.note: The patikam states that a former deed comes in wrath and makes its doer eat its fruit; here the narrator uses the same words (ஊழ்வினை, உருத்து) for the moment Kovalan leaves Madhavi.
links.teaches: The first time the narrative names the patikam's third moral at work, the deed ripens not in a crime or a court but in a lover mishearing a song, so the epic's karma enters the story through a private misjudgement long before Madurai.

links.note: Here the narrator gives Kovalan's break with Madhavi to his ripening deed; when he returns to Kannaki he gives his ruin to his own play with a deceitful woman (சலதி) and is ashamed.
links.teaches: The same break has two causes in two voices, karma in the narrator's and Madhavi's deceit in Kovalan's, so the epic lets its hero blame the woman while its own frame says the fault came from his past deed.

links.note: The couplet says a fate of loss makes a man foolish; the epic shows Kovalan, his deed ripening, take a sung convention for a confession and leave.
links.teaches: The epic supplies the mechanism the couplet only asserts: ripening fate does its work by making a man misread what is in front of him, here a song in an assumed voice, so the folly is the means of the loss.

gains.a: the epic's ஊழ்வினை gains a precise maxim for how it works on Kovalan, through a loss of judgement rather than an outside blow
gains.b: the couplet's abstract 'fate that makes foolish' gains a concrete case of what the folly looks like and what it costs

links.note: Kovalan sang the girls' charge that a man who swore by the sea god and broke his oath is without virtue; Madhavi's last song bows to the sea god and asks it to bear a false oath.
links.teaches: The two singers take opposite stances to the same broken oath before the same god, his to condemn and hers to plead for pardon, and the plea, left without a named oath-breaker, is what Kovalan hears as her guilt.

links.note: In the Ainkurunuru the friend says the girl's sickness is not the ford-spirit's doing but the man's oath; Madhavi's heroine asks the sea god not to punish the false oath sworn in the grove.
links.teaches: Both rest on the belief that a water deity punishes a false love-oath, but where the Sangam friend turns that belief against the man, the epic's heroine asks the god to spare him, so the same belief serves blame in one and loyal forgiveness in the other.

gains.a: the epic song gains the background belief that makes its plea meaningful: an oath sworn at the water draws the god's affliction
gains.b: the Ainkurunuru poem's belief gains a second use, as something a wronged woman can ask the god to withhold

links.note: The Kural's woman asks the bewildered evening whether its mate is as hard as hers; Madhavi's heroine asks whether this bewildering evening (மருள்மாலை) exists in the land of the man who left.
links.teaches: Both put to evening a question that is really about the absent man's hardness, and the epic sets that question in a performance before a lover who is present, showing how the convention can be heard as a personal charge.

gains.a: the epic stanza gains a known form, the address to evening, which marks it as a conventional lament rather than Madhavi's confession
gains.b: the couplet gains a dramatic setting in which its question is sung aloud and misheard, with consequences for the singer

links.note: The Kural says that when evening comes the whole town reels and suffers; Madhavi's heroine says the world shuts its eyes and, if evening and her husband are such, the world has become poor.
links.teaches: Both widen one woman's evening grief to the whole settlement, and the epic adds the lover himself to the cause, so the poverty of the world is laid as much on the husband's nature as on the hour.

gains.a: the epic stanza gains a Kural precedent for making the world share the lament
gains.b: the couplet's reeling town gains a named cause in the husband, which the couplet leaves out

links.note: The Kural makes the herdsman's flute evening's envoy and killing weapon; Madhavi's heroine says evening has struck the fishers' palai and bids it, if so skilled in melody, take her life.
links.teaches: In both the music of dusk is the instrument that kills the parted woman, but in the epic the song is sung on a yazh by a musician, so the deadly melody of evening is the singer's own art turned on herself.

gains.a: the epic stanza gains a precedent for evening's music as a weapon, which explains why the singer offers her life to a melody
gains.b: the couplet's image gains a second landscape, the fishers' shore in place of the herders' pasture, and a singer who is herself the musician

links.note: Kovalan sang of a conch that ploughed through a girl's sand-play and left her grieving; Madhavi sings of a man who came by the backwater, spoiled their sand-play and went.
links.teaches: Madhavi takes Kovalan's own image and puts a man in place of the conch, so the spoiled sand-play changes from a picture of a girl's charm into a charge of desertion, the answer-song turning his playful scene against the lover.

new_concepts.gloss: music: the lute, melody, mode and the sounds compared to them
new_concepts.label_source: the label is the house id used in chapter 8 of this book; this chapter's units name the yazh and its modes (யாழ் line 289, இசை line 268, பாலை line 268)

source_issues: Line 284 reads பூக்கமழ் கனலில் (in the flower-fragrant fire); the setting and the song cycle suggest கானலில் (in the shore grove), and the line may be faulty.
Lines 262 and 263 are the same line; it is the refrain of the form, as show flags, not a doubling.
